title: Breadth First Search (BFS): Visualized and Explained
beats: Shortest paths from a start vertex; intuition, implementation, flood fill application
Balls with strings: pull vertex 0 up, strings tighten, levels appear
Extend intuition to a messier graph: visit distance-1 then distance-2
Why shortest path is found upon first visit; equal edge weights; many valid orders
Implementation is DFS iterative with a queue instead of a stack
Trace queue step by step on small graph including already-marked pops
Flood fill: grid of integers, same-value connectivity
Paint bucket tool in MS Paint
It is a graph problem in disguise; grid pixels as vertices, edges to neighbours
Code: queue, visited set, recolour, neighbours function with bounds checks
Takeaway: change of perspective makes it a graph problem

metrics.examples: 1 simple graph (balls and strings), 1 larger graph, queue trace, 5x5 image flood fill with two start points

new_moves.name: problem-in-disguise
new_moves.what: Present a familiar-looking non-graph problem then reveal it reduces to the algorithm just taught

new_moves.name: physical-model-as-proof-sketch
new_moves.what: Strings pulled tight make levels visible and imply shortest paths

theory: A physical analogy (balls on strings) gives the whole structure of the algorithm and its key property in under a minute, then the implementation is introduced as a minimal diff on a previous video's code. The application recasts a familiar tool, paint bucket, as the algorithm.
velocity: Scene builder: physics-style 'pull the graph' animation as a reusable analogy scene for layered traversal
Orchestrator: when a prior concept is known, present new algorithm as a diff against it and diff highlight in the code view
Playbook: 'disguise' application at end, ask learner which vertex/edge model fits before reveal
